title: Dominic Culver’s Homepage
text:
About Me
I am a mathematician by training and I got my PhD in 2017 from the University of Notre Dame. I then went on to do postdocs first at the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign, and then another postdoc at the Max Planck Institute for Mathematics in Bonn Germany. My mathematical research interests were all within stable homotopy theory, and I was particularly interested in using ideas around elliptic curves and modular forms to understand complex structures in the stable homotopy groups of spheres.
In 2023, I decided to take the leap and transition into tech. I worked at an early legal AI startup for a year and half where I learned a lot of cool things about software and LLMs. My current interests are around ML and AI broadly, and NLP and LLMs more specifically. I am interested in building new and exciting things with these technologies while also using mathematical background to better understand LLMs in theory.
I currently work at Apple as an AIML Resident. I am also always happy to collaborate or discuss research ideas, please feel free to peruse my website and reach out!

title: Hello, World!
text:
Welcome to my new blog!
I am a mathematician turned AI enthusiast, and I am excited to start sharing my thoughts and experiences here. For this first post I wanted to share a bit about myself and what you can expect from this blog.

title: Hello, World!
text:
About Me
I completed my PhD in mathematics in 2017 at the University of Notre Dame, where I worked with Mark Behrens and wrote a thesis in stable homotopy theory. After that, I did two postdocs: one at the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign, and another at the Max Planck Institute for Mathematics in Bonn, Germany. My research focused primarily on chromatic homotopy theory broadly, and on using the spectrum of topological modular forms to understand the stable homotopy groups of spheres in particular. During my time in academia, I taught a variety of courses at both the undergraduate and graduate levels, including algebra, topology, and homotopy theory.
In 2023, I made the decision to transition from academia to the tech industry. I joined an early-stage legal AI startup where I worked on building AI systems and applications. I got to work on a lot of cool things with cool people, and I learned a lot about software development, machine learning, and natural language processing. It is amazing to think about how far AI has come in just a few years, and I am excited to be part of this rapidly evolving field.

title: Hello, World!
text:
What to Expect
For the moment, I plan to use this blog as a platform to share my thoughts on various topics related to AI and machine learning, though there may be the occasional mathematically focused post as well 😉. For now, I will be writing predominately about different papers I encounter in the wild, interesting developments in the field, and my personal experiences and insights as I continue to learn and grow in this new domain.
Comments and feedback are always welcome, and I hope to foster a community of like-minded individuals who are passionate about AI, machine learning, and the intersection of these fields with mathematics.
Happy reading, and stay tuned for more posts! If you have any suggestions for topics you’d like me to cover, feel free to reach out! 👋

title: Byte Latent Transformers
text:
Introduction
Earlier this year, a very interesting research article came out from a team at Meta. In this paper, they propose a new transformers-based architecture for LLMs which operates at the level of bytes rather than at the level of tokens, thus being dubbed the Byte Latent Transformer (BLT for short 🥪). One of the central motivations for their proposal is that current tokenization-based approaches to LLMs are inefficient, in as far as tokenization is a pre-computed grouping of bytes which doesn’t necessarily allocate compute resources intelligently based on the context. To justify their new architecture, they show the results from several experiments which shows that their model performs as well as (or even better in some instances) other frontier models. My goals for this post is:

Explain in greater detail the motivation to work on bytes
Explain the model architecture and how training and inference work.
Discuss the empirical studies done by the authors as the relate to performance and scaling laws for their architecture.
Raise some questions that I had from reading the paper.

This post is by no means a substitute for reading the paper, and I highly encourage you to go do so. However, I hope this post helps in some small way. And of course, it should go without saying, that any mistakes are mine and mine alone, and feel free to email me if you have any corrections.


LLMs and Tokenization
Before getting into the nitty-gritty of the BLT architecture it seems best to remind ourselves how LLMs currently work and where this brings up bottlenecks and pitfalls.  Of main concern for the BLT paper, in particular, is the reliance on tokenization for LLMs. Below is a diagram which caricatures how LLMs currently work.





flowchart LR
  A[Input String] --> B[Tokenizer]
  B --> C[Sequence of Tokens]
  C --> D[Decoder-only Transformer]
  D --> E[Probability Distribution]
  E --> F[Next Token]






What is the purpose of the tokenizer in the first place? Transformers take in tensors and output tensors. However, when using a transformer, we want to input a string of text. The purpose of the tokenizer is to bridge this gap. It takes in an input string and partitions the string into substrings known as tokens. These tokens, in turn, are mapped onto integers, and the whole input string is turned into an array of integers. We can tensorize this array, thereby creating an object which the transformer can operate on.
There are several tokenizers out there, but all tokenizers use some sort of algorithm (e.g. Byte Pair Encoding) and a corpus of text to construct the tokens. Moreover, the tokenizer is trained separately and before any sort of training takes place for the LLM itself. This means, in particular, that the tokenizer being used has a fixed token space. In the case of GPT-2 example, the tokenizer used was trained using the BPE algorithm and has 50,257 tokens.
After converting an input text into an array of integers, we feed that into the LLM and get an output tensor which is a probability distribution over the token space. In the case of GPT-2, then, this would be a 50,257-vector.
Let’s go through this diagram step-by-step with a running example using the GPT-2 tokenizer. Suppose that the input sentence is "The cat is on the". This is tokenized into the following sequence: ["The", " cat", " is", " on", " the"].
These are then turned into a tensor array of integers [464, 3797, 318, 319, 262]. Feeding these into the transformer, we get an output tensor of length 50,257. Taking the argmax of this probability tensor we are likely to get the integer 2603, which corresponds to the token " mat". Note how the tokenizer determines the type of output the transformer will output. In the case of an LLM, the fact that we use a tokenizer dictates that we must output a probability distribution from which we sample.
The use of tokenizers come with certain trade-offs. For one, they have a fixed token space as mentioned earlier. This results in the tokenizer not being able to recognize sequences of characters which are out of sample.
